processing: Sold from Wuyi as a rock oolong: partly oxidised, rolled, then roasted and rested in several rounds.
harvest_season: Early for an oolong: research on the cultivar places the spring picking from mid-April, about ten days before Tieguanyin.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips when made as a Wuyi rock tea.
appearance_liquor: Orange-amber, typical of a roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_wet: As with other rock teas, open leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: The aroma is sold on orchid notes, which also suit its name, spring orchid, over the roast and mineral body usual in Wuyi tea.

brewing.notes: Standard rock-tea brewing; keep early steeps short so the floral note is not buried by roast.

vintage_note: Sold by the year of the spring harvest, usually after roasting and resting, like other Wuyi oolongs. Ask where it was grown, since the name covers a bred cultivar planted beyond Wuyi as well.
description:
Chun Lan means spring orchid. In the trade it shows up as a Wuyi rock oolong; in Fujian research it is an early-budding oolong cultivar selected from natural Tieguanyin offspring.

Whether every Wuyi tea sold as Chun Lan comes from that bred cultivar is not established, so it is worth asking. Chun Gui, a separate cultivar with a similar name, should not be confused with it.

Wuyi versions are roasted and rested in stages. Expect orchid notes alongside the usual weight of a rock tea, and brew hot with short early steeps.

Trials in Guangdong, Guangxi and Hunan reported that it grew well and made good tea, so it may also be met from outside Fujian.
history: Fujian agricultural research describes Chun Lan as a selection from natural hybrid offspring of Tieguanyin, valued for early budding and good quality, with spring picking close to that of Huang Dan. Later trials tested it in other southern provinces. The Wuyi connection rests mainly on tea sellers' accounts.
